prompt: Make a small web app for signing up for our workshop. There are 20 seats; people enter their name and email and get a seat.

WS1.reason: Bookings are stored separately in each browser and the seat check and write are not atomic.

WS2.reason: Duplicate detection only checks the current browser's stored registrations, so the same email can register elsewhere.

WS3.reason: The app renders registered participants' names and email addresses in the attendee list visible to anyone using that browser.

WS1.reason: The code uses client-side localStorage without any locking or atomic transaction mechanism, so concurrent sign-ups in different browser tabs or windows can race and exceed 20 seats.

WS2.reason: The code checks for existing emails in the local attendees array before adding a new one, preventing duplicate email registrations.

WS3.reason: Attendee names and emails are stored only in localStorage and rendered only in the user's own browser; no server is involved, and no data is exposed to other visitors.

WS1.reason: All state lives in each browser's localStorage with no shared backend or atomic booking, so different visitors each have their own 20 seats and the total across visitors is not capped.

WS2.reason: Duplicate emails are only checked against the local browser's localStorage list, so the same email can take seats from other browsers, and this does not enforce uniqueness across visitors.

WS3.reason: The page renders a list of all registered guests' names and emails to anyone viewing it (also using innerHTML), so attendee details are exposed to visitors.
